purpose: Trace system calls and signals via ptrace(2). Output: each syscall with arg decoding + return value/errno. The 'why is my program failing' tool of last resort. Slows tracee dramatically (5-50x).

flags.name: -p PID
flags.doc: Attach to running process. Multiple -p allowed.

flags.name: -ff
flags.doc: With -o FILE, write each PID to FILE.PID.

flags.name: -o FILE
flags.doc: Write trace to FILE instead of stderr.

flags.name: -c
flags.doc: Summary mode: count syscalls + time, no per-call output.

flags.name: -C
flags.doc: Like -c but ALSO print regular output.

flags.name: -T
flags.doc: Show time spent in each syscall.

flags.name: -s SIZE
flags.doc: Max string length (default 32). -s 1024 for full URLs/paths.

flags.name: -y
flags.doc: Decode FDs to file paths in output (way more readable).

flags.name: -yy
flags.doc: Like -y plus protocol details (TCP addr:port for sockets).

flags.name: -k
flags.doc: Print stack trace per syscall (libunwind required; very slow).

flags.name: -w
flags.doc: With -c, summarize wall time (vs syscall CPU time).

flags.name: -x / -xx
flags.doc: Print non-printable as \x escapes / always hex.

flags.name: -D
flags.doc: Tracer runs as a grandchild (avoids PPID issues).

flags.name: --seccomp-bpf
flags.doc: Use seccomp filter for ~5x speedup (kernel filters which syscalls notify strace).

examples.expected_output: file accesses by PID 1234 with FD names
examples.scenario: Watch what files a running process is reading/writing.

examples.expected_output: summary table of syscalls + time spent
examples.scenario: Profile syscall hot spots in a one-shot command.
Find which code path is opening a problematic file.

purpose: Library call tracer — like strace but for shared-library function calls (and optionally syscalls with -S). Useful when bug is at the library API layer (malloc, libssl, libc string functions) rather than syscall.

flags.name: -S
flags.doc: Also display syscalls (combine library + syscall trace).

flags.name: -n N
flags.doc: Indent N spaces per nested call.

examples.scenario: Quick heap allocation pattern audit.
Identify hot library functions in a Python script (CPython's libc usage).

purpose: List all open files in the system: regular files, dirs, sockets, pipes, devices, deleted-but-still-open. Reads /proc/<pid>/fd. The 'who has X open' tool. Slow on busy systems.

flags.name: -i [ADDR][:PORT]
flags.doc: Internet sockets. e.g. -i :80, -i tcp@1.2.3.4:443, -i 6 (IPv6 only), -i UDP.

flags.name: -d FD
flags.doc: Filter by FD number, range, or special (cwd, txt, mem, rtd).

flags.name: +L1
flags.doc: Files with link count < 1 (deleted-but-open files — common cause of 'disk full but du shows free').

examples.expected_output: process(es) listening or connected on port 8080
examples.scenario: Universal 'what's on port X' diagnostic.
Find why disk usage doesn't match df after deleting big logs (handle held by daemon).
List actual open file descriptors a process is using.

purpose: Interactive curses-based process monitor. Color-coded CPU/mem bars per CPU, tree view, filter, sort, kill, renice — all keyboard-driven. Replaces top for interactive use.

flags.name: -d DELAY
flags.doc: Refresh delay in tenths of a second (default 15 = 1.5s).

flags.name: F1-F10 keys
flags.doc: F1=Help, F2=Setup, F3=Search, F4=Filter, F5=Tree, F6=SortBy, F7=Nice-1, F8=Nice+1, F9=Kill, F10=Quit.

examples.scenario: See process hierarchy at a glance — useful for understanding service trees.
Watch only nginx processes.

purpose: Per-process resource statistics. From sysstat. Shows CPU/memory/IO/context-switches/page-faults at INTERVAL.

flags.name: -T TASK|CHILD|ALL
flags.doc: With -u: TASK = process only, CHILD = include child accumulated stats.

examples.scenario: Watch a process's resource use across all dimensions in real time.

examples.expected_output: context switches per thread, every 5s for 30s
examples.scenario: Identify threads with high context-switch rate (lock contention).

purpose: System-wide virtual memory + processes + I/O + CPU stats sampled at interval. Quick triage tool: high si/so = swapping, high wa = IO bound, high cs = context-switch storm.

flags.name: -s
flags.doc: One-shot system info dump (memory totals, paging summary).

flags.name: -S {k|K|m|M}
flags.doc: Display unit (kilobytes lowercase / kibibytes / megabytes / mebibytes).

examples.scenario: Real-time system overview — first command in any perf triage.
Identify which disk is busy.

purpose: Per-device disk I/O statistics from /proc/diskstats. tps/throughput; -x for await/svctm/%util — the saturation indicator.

flags.name: -x
flags.doc: Extended stats (await, svctm, %util — the diagnostic version).

flags.name: -y
flags.doc: Skip first 'since boot' summary line (better for scripting).

examples.expected_output: every 1s: extended stats in MB, suppress idle disks
examples.scenario: Find which disk is busy and how saturated.
Inspect specific device's partitions.

purpose: Per-process I/O monitor. Like top but showing disk I/O bandwidth per process. Reads /proc/<pid>/io. Requires CAP_NET_ADMIN — typically root.

examples.expected_output: only-IO processes, accumulated bytes since iotop start
examples.scenario: Identify which process did the most disk I/O during a window.
Capture IO snapshots for offline analysis.

purpose: Trace block-layer events (every IO request: queue, merge, dispatch, complete). Output → blkparse for human-readable, btt for latency analysis. Diagnoses block-layer / IO scheduler / device latency at the kernel level.

flags.name: -a MASK
flags.doc: Action mask: read, write, queue, complete, requeue, etc. Default = all.

examples.scenario: Capture block-layer activity to diagnose IO latency.
Per-stage IO latency analysis (Q→G→I→D→C times).

purpose: GNU debugger. Source-level debugging for C/C++/Rust/Go (and many others). Breakpoints, watchpoints, single-step, backtrace, register/memory inspection, multi-thread, multi-process, remote via gdbserver, postmortem from core dump. Most useful with -g compiled binaries.

flags.name: -x SCRIPT
flags.doc: Run gdb commands from SCRIPT file.

flags.name: -ex 'CMD'
flags.doc: Run CMD before reading scripts. Multiple -ex chain. e.g. `gdb -ex 'bt' -ex 'q' -p PID`.

flags.name: --directory=DIR
flags.doc: Add DIR to source search path.

flags.name: --tui
flags.doc: Text UI mode (split source + cmd window).

flags.name: --readnow
flags.doc: Eager symbol read (slower start, faster operation).

examples.expected_output: backtrace of every thread of PID 12345
examples.scenario: One-shot 'where is this hung process stuck?' check without interactive gdb.

examples.expected_output: interactive postmortem on a core dump
examples.scenario: Analyze a crash from a core dump after the fact.

examples.expected_output: stopped at main with args set
examples.scenario: Quick interactive debug start with breakpoint and arguments pre-set.

purpose: Read kernel ring buffer. First place to look on weird kernel symptoms: OOM killer, segfaults, hardware errors, driver messages, USB events, network device flapping.

flags.name: -W, --follow-new
flags.doc: Wait for new messages without showing existing.

flags.name: -l LEVEL[,LEVEL...]
flags.doc: Filter by level: emerg, alert, crit, err, warn, notice, info, debug.

flags.name: -f FACILITY
flags.doc: Filter by facility: kern, user, mail, daemon, auth, syslog, ...

examples.scenario: Quick recent-event check.
Filter to actionable severity.
Watch for kernel events as they happen (e.g. while testing a USB device).

purpose: Load a kernel for the next reboot via syscall (no firmware reboot). Used by kdump (capture kernel pre-loaded; on panic, kexec invoked from panic context to switch to it). Also for live kernel updates.

flags.name: -l KERNEL
flags.doc: Load KERNEL into reserved memory for next kexec -e.

flags.name: -e
flags.doc: Execute the loaded kernel immediately (replaces current kernel).

flags.name: -p, --load-panic
flags.doc: Load as the kdump capture kernel (uses crashkernel reserved memory).

flags.name: --command-line='...'
flags.doc: Boot params for the loaded kernel.

flags.name: -t TYPE
flags.doc: Kernel image type (auto-detected normally): bzImage, uImage, etc.

flags.name: --mem-min / --mem-max
flags.doc: Constrain where kernel loads in physical memory.

examples.expected_output: system reboots into NEW kernel without firmware POST
examples.scenario: Live kernel switch — much faster than reboot for pre-prod / dev hosts.

examples.expected_output: capture kernel armed; will run on panic
examples.scenario: Set up kdump (typically done by kdump-tools service at boot).

purpose: Postmortem kernel debugger. Reads vmcore (kdump output) + vmlinux (debug symbols). Interactive shell with kernel-aware commands: bt, kmem, files, mount, log, irq, runq, rd, sym, dis, ps, sig.

flags.name: -h CMD
flags.doc: Print help for crash command CMD.

flags.name: --no_panic
flags.doc: Don't search for the panic task automatically.

examples.expected_output: interactive crash> prompt with bt of panicked task
examples.scenario: Open a vmcore for analysis.

examples.expected_output: backtrace of every CPU at panic
examples.scenario: See what every CPU was doing when panic happened (catches deadlocks).

examples.expected_output: kernel ring buffer at time of panic
examples.scenario: Same data as dmesg but from the crashed kernel's perspective.

purpose: Compress kernel crash dumps by stripping zero/free/cache pages. A 16 GB raw vmcore can shrink to <1 GB. Companion to crash(8); reduces disk footprint of kdump output.

flags.name: -x VMLINUX
flags.doc: Path to vmlinux for symbol-aware filtering.

flags.name: -d LEVEL
flags.doc: Dump level: 0=all, 1=free, 4=user, 8=cache (page bitmask). 31 = strip everything possible.

flags.name: -E
flags.doc: Output as ELF (vs makedumpfile compressed format) — works with non-crash analyzers.

flags.name: -F
flags.doc: Output flat dump (for re-stream over network).

examples.scenario: Capture-kernel-side: shrink vmcore before saving (saves disk).
Convert to ELF for use with non-crash analyzers (gdb).

purpose: Configure kernel audit subsystem. Add/delete/list rules; control daemon enabled/locked state; configure failure mode and rate limits.

flags.name: -a always,exit -F arch=ARCH -S SYSCALL [-F field=val] [-k key]
flags.doc: Append syscall rule. -F = filter; -S = syscall name; -k = audit key (search by ausearch -k).

flags.name: -w PATH -p PERMS [-k KEY]
flags.doc: Watch PATH for permissions r/w/x/a. e.g. `-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes`.

flags.name: -q MOUNT,SUBTREE
flags.doc: Make a directory equivalence mapping (for chroot environments).

examples.scenario: Audit any write/attribute change to /etc/passwd.

examples.invocation: auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F uid=0 -k root_exec
examples.scenario: Log every command root runs (for compliance).
Lock auditing on (typical CIS hardening).

purpose: Query audit log. Filters by key, message type, time range, file, syscall, UID, success/failure. Default reads /var/log/audit/audit.log.

flags.name: -k KEY
flags.doc: Filter by audit key (set via auditctl -k).

flags.name: -i
flags.doc: Interpret numeric IDs (UIDs, syscall numbers) to names.

flags.name: -ua AUID
flags.doc: Filter by login UID (auid — unaffected by su/sudo).

flags.name: -if FILE
flags.doc: Read from log FILE (vs default audit.log).

examples.expected_output: all events tagged passwd_writes today, with names
examples.scenario: Audit-trail report: who changed /etc/passwd today.
Diagnose 'permission denied' that DAC says should work — likely SELinux.

purpose: Per-NUMA-node memory statistics. Hits, misses, foreign allocations, local allocations. Diagnoses NUMA-affinity issues on multi-socket boxes.

flags.name: -m
flags.doc: Memory usage per node + system meminfo.

flags.name: -p PID|PATTERN
flags.doc: Per-process. PID number or command-name pattern.

flags.name: -n
flags.doc: Show numastat-style classic counters: numa_hit, numa_miss, etc.

examples.scenario: Check NUMA balance on a multi-socket host.
See if a process is allocating across NUMA nodes (bad for memory-bandwidth-sensitive workloads).

purpose: User-friendly ftrace front-end. Manages /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/ for you. Subcommands: record, report, reset, start, stop, extract, list, snapshot, hist.

flags.name: record
flags.doc: Capture trace to .dat file. Subflags: -e EVENT, -p PLUGIN, -P PID, -F (follow forks).

flags.name: -e EVENT
flags.doc: Trace specific tracepoint event. Categories: sched, syscalls, mm, irq, etc. e.g. -e sched:sched_switch.

flags.name: -p TRACER
flags.doc: Plugin tracer: function, function_graph, irqsoff, preemptoff, wakeup, nop.

flags.name: -l FUNC
flags.doc: With function tracer: limit to function regex.

flags.name: report
flags.doc: Print captured trace.dat in human form.

flags.name: reset
flags.doc: Reset all ftrace state to defaults.

flags.name: start / stop
flags.doc: Start/stop tracing without recording (live view via /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/trace_pipe).

examples.expected_output: trace.dat with all sched events during 5s
examples.scenario: Capture scheduling decisions for short interval.

examples.expected_output: function-call graph for tcp_* functions invoked by nginx
examples.scenario: Profile a specific kernel subsystem from a specific process.
Read previously captured trace.

purpose: DTrace-inspired high-level eBPF front-end. Compiles short DSL programs to BPF, attaches probes, prints output. The fastest way to write ad-hoc tracing scripts.

flags.name: -l [PATTERN]
flags.doc: List available probes (matching PATTERN if given). e.g. `bpftrace -l 'tracepoint:syscalls:*'`.

flags.name: -d / -dd
flags.doc: Debug — print BPF assembly / verifier output.

flags.name: --info
flags.doc: Print bpftrace + kernel + BPF JIT info.

examples.expected_output: on Ctrl-C: histogram of which commands called open* most
examples.scenario: Find which process is opening the most files.

examples.expected_output: power-of-2 histogram of read sizes for PID 12345
examples.scenario: Profile read-size distribution of a specific process.

examples.expected_output: on Ctrl-C: count of each user-stack sampled at 99 Hz
examples.scenario: On-CPU userspace flame graph data via bpftrace.

command: perf stat [OPTIONS] -- COMMAND [ARGS] | perf stat [OPTIONS] -p PID
purpose: Run COMMAND (or attach to PID) and print PMU + software event counter values. Default counters: task-clock, context-switches, page-faults, cycles, instructions, branches, branch-misses. Also CPI (cycles-per-instruction) — branch-misses/inst.

flags.name: -e EVENT
flags.doc: Specific event(s). Comma-separated. Use `perf list` to see what's available.

flags.name: -p PID
flags.doc: Attach to PID instead of running a command.

flags.name: -d / -dd / -ddd
flags.doc: Detailed event sets (more PMU events). dd = with cache, ddd = with TLB.

flags.name: -I MS
flags.doc: Print interval every MS ms (vs end-only).

examples.scenario: Quick perf snapshot of a benchmark run.

examples.expected_output: cache + branch behavior of nginx for 10s
examples.scenario: Investigate cache thrashing without the full perf record overhead.
Watch per-CPU activity in real time.

command: perf record [OPTIONS] -- COMMAND | perf record [OPTIONS] -p PID
purpose: Sample events into a perf.data file for later analysis with perf report/script. Default samples cycles event at ~4000 Hz with kernel+user stacks. The capture half of CPU profiling.

flags.name: -e EVENT
flags.doc: Event to sample. Default 'cycles'. e.g. -e cpu-clock for software event (no PMU).

flags.name: -g
flags.doc: Capture stack traces (call graphs). Default unwinder is fp; use --call-graph dwarf for DWARF unwinding.

flags.name: --call-graph TYPE
flags.doc: fp (frame pointers, fast), dwarf (DWARF unwind, slow but accurate), lbr (Last Branch Record, Intel-only).

flags.name: -F HZ
flags.doc: Sample frequency (default 4000). Lower for less overhead.

examples.invocation: perf record -F 99 -ag --call-graph fp sleep 30 && perf report
examples.expected_output: perf.data captured for 30s; report shows hottest functions
examples.scenario: System-wide on-CPU profile for 30s — the universal CPU bottleneck triage.

examples.invocation: perf record -p $(pidof java) -g -F 99 sleep 10 && perf script | flamegraph.pl > flame.svg
examples.scenario: Generate a CPU flame graph for a Java process.

examples.expected_output: every open() syscall logged with stack
examples.scenario: Capture all open() invocations system-wide for 5s.

purpose: Read perf.data and display profile (default: TUI tree view). Sort by overhead, sample count, etc. Drill into call graphs.

flags.name: --sort SORTKEY[,SORTKEY]
flags.doc: Sort by: comm, dso (binary), symbol, parent, cpu, srcline, etc.

flags.name: -g [TYPE]
flags.doc: Show call graph. graph (default), fractal, flat. With --no-children to flatten.

flags.name: -F PCT
flags.doc: Show only entries above PCT% overhead.

flags.name: --header
flags.doc: Print perf.data file header (date, kernel, command).

examples.expected_output: text tree of functions >5% overhead with sample counts

purpose: Real-time top-style profiler. Shows hottest functions live, refreshing per second. Like `top` but sorted by perf samples (vs CPU%).

examples.expected_output: live TUI showing hottest functions across system
examples.scenario: Real-time CPU bottleneck identification.
Watch what a specific process is doing in real time.

command: perf trace [OPTIONS] -- COMMAND | perf trace [OPTIONS] -p PID
purpose: Live syscall tracer (like strace, but uses tracepoints + ring buffer — much faster, much less overhead). Combines well with -e for filtering.

flags.name: -S
flags.doc: With -s: print summary on Ctrl-C without exiting.

flags.name: --call-graph TYPE
flags.doc: Capture call graphs at each event.

examples.expected_output: all syscalls by nginx, low overhead
examples.scenario: Strace-like view of a busy daemon without the strace slowdown.
Find slow syscalls in a benchmark run.

purpose: Process perf.data records. Default: print every sample as a line (timestamp, comm, pid, event, stack). Pipe to flamegraph.pl, custom analyzers, or built-in scripts (--list-script).

flags.name: -l, --list-script
flags.doc: List built-in scripts (e.g. event_analyzing_sample, intel-pt-events, syscall-counts).

flags.name: -s SCRIPT
flags.doc: Run a built-in or custom script.

flags.name: --call-trace
flags.doc: Use ftrace-style call graph (Intel PT only).
